promptText: For `User user = new User();`, where does the User object live versus where does the `user` reference variable live, and which memory error corresponds to exhausting each region?
options: The object lives on the shared Heap (exhaustion causes OutOfMemoryError); the reference lives on the current thread's Stack (exhaustion causes StackOverflowError)
Both the object and the reference live on the Heap, since Java has no separate stack memory region
The object lives on the Stack while the reference lives on the Heap, the reverse of the common assumption
Both live in Metaspace, which is why Metaspace exhaustion is the most common OutOfMemoryError variant
explanation: The Heap is the shared region where all object instances live and where GC operates; each thread's Stack holds method frames and local variables, including references that merely point at heap objects -- exhausting the shared heap throws OutOfMemoryError, while exhausting one thread's private stack (typically via deep recursion) throws StackOverflowError.

promptText: How do the JDK, JRE, and JVM relate to each other?
options: They are nested layers: the JDK contains the JRE plus development tools (javac, jar, jstack); the JRE contains the JVM plus the core class libraries needed to run an application; the JVM is the engine that actually executes bytecode
They are three independent, interchangeable ways to run Java code, and only one needs to be installed
The JRE contains the JDK, which in turn contains the JVM, the reverse of the common ordering
The JVM is a compiler that produces the JRE, which is then packaged into the JDK for distribution
explanation: JDK is for building applications (it bundles the JRE plus compiler and diagnostic tools), JRE is for running them (JVM plus libraries, no compiler), and the JVM is the abstract machine at the core that actually interprets/JIT-compiles and executes bytecode -- getting the nesting direction backwards is a common but incorrect answer.

promptText: Why did Java 8 replace PermGen with Metaspace, and what specific production problem did this solve?
options: Metaspace lives in native memory and grows dynamically rather than being a fixed-size region carved out of the Java heap, which eliminated the chronic OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space failures common in servers that repeatedly loaded and reloaded classes
Metaspace was introduced purely to improve JIT compilation speed and has no relationship to class metadata storage
PermGen was removed because it stored object instances, which Metaspace now stores more efficiently on the heap
Metaspace guarantees that OutOfMemoryError can never occur again, unlike PermGen which had a hard size limit
explanation: PermGen's fixed, small, heap-bounded size made it a frequent failure point for applications that loaded many classes or leaked classloaders during redeploys; Metaspace solves this by living in native memory and growing dynamically by default, though it can still be exhausted (OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace) from classloader leaks, so a ceiling via -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is still advisable in long-lived services.

promptText: An object becomes unreachable from any GC Root at time T, but is only actually reclaimed at time T+5 seconds. Why is this normal, and what does calling System.gc() actually guarantee?
options: Eligibility for collection and the actual collection are separate events -- the JVM decides when to run a GC cycle (typically when a region fills up); System.gc() is only a hint the JVM is free to ignore, not a guarantee
This indicates a bug, because a genuinely unreachable object must be reclaimed within one JVM instruction cycle by specification
System.gc() always forces an immediate, synchronous Full GC in every JVM implementation
Eligibility only applies to objects in the Old Generation; Young Generation objects are always reclaimed instantly upon becoming unreachable
explanation: Becoming eligible only means the JVM MAY collect the object; the actual reclaim happens whenever the collector next runs, which could be immediate or much later depending on allocation pressure -- this is exactly why code correctness should never depend on precisely when an object is collected, and why System.gc() is treated as an unreliable hint rather than a command.

promptText: OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError are often confused. What is the cleanest way to distinguish them?
options: OutOfMemoryError is a heap-region problem typically caused by a memory leak or undersized heap; StackOverflowError is a per-thread stack problem almost always caused by runaway/infinite recursion
OutOfMemoryError is always caused by recursion, while StackOverflowError is always caused by a memory leak
Both errors refer to the exact same underlying condition and are simply two names used interchangeably by different JVM vendors
StackOverflowError only occurs in multi-threaded applications, while OutOfMemoryError only occurs in single-threaded ones
explanation: The two originate in entirely different memory regions: OOM concerns the shared heap (or related native areas) running out of allocatable space, usually from retained objects or an undersized heap, while SOE concerns a single thread's private call stack overflowing from deeply nested or infinite recursive calls -- heap problem/retention bug versus stack problem/recursion bug.

promptText: Why can a Java application still suffer a "memory leak" even though the JVM has automatic garbage collection?
options: GC only reclaims objects that are unreachable; if code unintentionally keeps a reference to an object it no longer needs (e.g. in a static collection), the object stays reachable and the GC correctly, but uselessly, keeps it alive forever
Garbage collection in Java only runs once per application lifetime, so anything allocated after that point is never collected
Java memory leaks are actually native memory leaks caused entirely by JNI code, never by pure Java code
The GC intentionally skips objects larger than a certain size threshold to save collection time
explanation: A Java "leak" is a logical leak, not a technical failure of the collector: the memory is still referenced (often from a long-lived GC Root like a static field, an unbounded cache, or a registered listener that's never removed) so the GC correctly refuses to reclaim it, even though the application has no further use for it.

promptText: Generational garbage collection splits the heap into Young and Old generations based on the "weak generational hypothesis." What does this hypothesis claim, and how does it justify collecting the Young Generation far more often than the Old?
options: Most objects die young while the few that survive tend to live a long time, so concentrating short-lived objects in a small, frequently-collected region (Young Gen) is cheap, while the Old Generation -- holding objects that already proved long-lived -- needs collection only rarely
All objects have an equal, random chance of becoming garbage regardless of age, so generational splitting is purely a historical convention with no performance basis
Objects in the Old Generation are inherently faster to collect than objects in the Young Generation because they are fewer in number
The hypothesis claims that object lifetime correlates with object size, so generations are split by size rather than by age
explanation: This empirical observation is the entire justification for the generational design: because the vast majority of allocated objects (like per-request DTOs and temporary collections) become garbage almost immediately, a Minor GC can cheaply discard most of Eden's contents wholesale and only copy out the small number of survivors, while the rarely-changing Old Generation is left alone until it genuinely needs attention.

promptText: During a Minor GC, live objects are copied from Eden and the currently-active Survivor space into the other, currently-empty Survivor space, which then swap roles. Why does this design mean it's normal to see one Survivor space (S0 or S1) reporting zero usage in monitoring tools?
options: At any given moment, exactly one Survivor space is the active destination for the current cycle's survivors while the other sits empty by design, ready to receive the next cycle's copies -- this copying approach also compacts live objects and eliminates fragmentation
Reporting zero usage on one Survivor space always indicates a Survivor space has been corrupted and should be flagged as a bug
Both Survivor spaces should always show roughly equal, non-zero usage; zero usage means the JVM has disabled generational collection entirely
The empty Survivor space is reserved exclusively for objects that are about to be promoted to the Old Generation, not for normal copying
explanation: The ping-pong Survivor design deliberately keeps one space empty between cycles: each Minor GC copies survivors from Eden plus the in-use Survivor space into the other (empty) one, then wipes the vacated regions, which both compacts memory and lets the JVM track each object's survival count toward the tenuring threshold -- so a Survivor showing zero usage is expected, not a fault.

promptText: Why does the JVM use reachability analysis from GC Roots instead of simple reference counting to determine garbage, and what specific case does this choice handle correctly?
options: Reference counting cannot correctly detect two objects that reference only each other but are unreachable from any GC Root (a cycle); reachability analysis traces live references outward from GC Roots and correctly identifies such a cycle as garbage since neither object is reached from the trace
Reference counting is actually faster and more accurate, but reachability analysis is used only because it's simpler to implement
Both techniques handle cyclic references identically; the JVM's choice is purely a historical accident from early Java versions
Reachability analysis is used only for the Old Generation, while reference counting is used for the Young Generation
explanation: A pure reference-counting scheme would see each object in a mutual-reference cycle holding a count of 1 (from the other) and never reach zero, even though the pair is completely unreachable from the running program; by instead tracing outward from trusted anchors (GC Roots: local variables, static fields, active threads, JNI references) and marking everything reached as live, the JVM correctly classifies an isolated cycle as garbage since nothing in it is ever reached from a root.

promptText: What is "premature promotion," and why does an undersized Young Generation make it worse?
options: If Eden or the Survivor spaces are too small, objects get promoted to the Old Generation before they've had a real chance to die, polluting Old with short-lived garbage and triggering more frequent, more expensive Old Generation (Major/Full) collections
Premature promotion means objects are moved to the Young Generation before being fully initialized, causing NullPointerExceptions later
An undersized Young Generation has no effect on promotion behavior; only the tenuring threshold setting affects when objects are promoted
Premature promotion only affects Metaspace sizing, not the heap's generational structure at all
explanation: Promotion is meant for objects that have proven themselves long-lived by surviving several Minor GCs, but when the Young Generation is too small, objects get pushed out to Old before they've had time to become garbage naturally; this pollutes the Old Generation with objects that would have died young, forcing more frequent and expensive Major/Full collections -- a key reason GC tuning often involves resizing the Young Generation rather than just the whole heap.

promptText: Both a Minor GC and a Full GC are "stop-the-world" events, yet a Minor GC is usually imperceptible while a Full GC can cause visible request timeouts. What actually accounts for this difference?
options: A Minor GC only touches the small, high-churn Young Generation and uses a cheap copying algorithm on a handful of survivors, while a Full GC walks the entire heap (Young + Old + typically Metaspace), which is larger and mostly full of live, densely-packed data that must be marked and compacted
A Minor GC does not actually pause any threads, while only a Full GC is a stop-the-world event
Minor GCs run on a background thread that never interrupts the application, unlike Full GCs which always run on the main application thread
The difference is purely a naming convention with no actual difference in the work performed or the pause duration
explanation: Both are technically stop-the-world pauses, but their scope and cost are wildly different: a Minor GC's small target region and copying-only-the-survivors approach make it fast enough to be nearly invisible, while a Full GC's comprehensive, whole-heap mark-and-compact pass on a region full of long-lived (mostly live) data is what produces the multi-second pauses that show up as API latency spikes and failed health checks.

promptText: Why does a `private static List<User> users = new ArrayList<>();` that is only ever appended to (never cleared) constitute a classic memory leak, even though the JVM's GC is working correctly?
options: The list is reachable from a GC Root (the class's static field) for the entire life of the application, so every User object added to it remains reachable and can never be collected, no matter how useless those Users become to the running program
ArrayList has an internal bug that causes it to leak memory whenever it resizes its backing array
static fields are automatically cleared by the JVM every time a Full GC runs, so this scenario is not actually a leak
The leak occurs only because ArrayList is not thread-safe, not because of the static field's reachability
explanation: static fields live for the entire application lifetime and are one of the canonical GC Roots, so anything reachable through them is permanently reachable and therefore permanently ineligible for collection; the fix is not a GC bug workaround but a design fix -- bound the collection, add eviction, or stop treating a raw static ArrayList as a cache.

promptText: How does G1 GC's region-based heap design differ fundamentally from the fixed contiguous Young/Old generations used by Serial or Parallel GC, and what capability does this enable?
options: G1 divides the heap into many equally-sized regions and dynamically labels each one as Eden, Survivor, or Old (a region's role can change between collections), which lets it collect the regions containing the most garbage first and pursue a tunable pause-time goal (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis) rather than being forced into a monolithic full-generation pass
G1 eliminates generations entirely and treats every object identically regardless of age, unlike Serial or Parallel GC
G1's regions are fixed at JVM startup and can never change their Eden/Survivor/Old label for the life of the process, identical to older collectors
G1 achieves low pause times by disabling stop-the-world pauses completely, unlike every other HotSpot collector
explanation: In Serial/Parallel GC, Young and Old are fixed, contiguous blocks of memory that must be collected as whole units; G1's uniform regions are just logical labels that can be reassigned between cycles, which is what lets it incrementally collect only the regions with the most reclaimable garbage ("Garbage First") and size its work to meet a soft pause-time target -- this region flexibility, not the elimination of generations or of stop-the-world pauses, is G1's real innovation.

promptText: When analyzing a heap dump in a tool like Eclipse MAT to find a leak, why is sorting by "retained size" more useful than sorting by "shallow size," and what does following the "path to GC Roots" from a dominator object reveal?
options: Shallow size is only the object itself, while retained size includes everything that would be freed if that object were collected (everything reachable only through it); the largest retained-size "dominator" objects show where memory is actually trapped, and tracing their path to GC Roots reveals exactly which field, static reference, or ThreadLocal is keeping that memory alive
Shallow size and retained size are always identical for every object, so the distinction is purely academic and has no practical effect on the analysis
Retained size only matters for primitive arrays; for regular objects, shallow size is always the more accurate measure of true memory impact
Path to GC Roots identifies which thread most recently allocated the object, not which reference is preventing its collection
explanation: A small object (low shallow size) can still be a dominator with enormous retained size if it's the sole entry point to a huge subgraph of otherwise-unreachable objects -- for example a single Map holding millions of cached entries; ranking by retained size surfaces exactly those objects, and tracing the reference chain back to a GC Root (a static field, a live thread's stack, or a ThreadLocal) tells you precisely which piece of code is responsible for the leak, rather than just how large the leaked data happens to be.

promptText: Why is a ThreadLocal value set on a request-handling thread in a pooled server (like Tomcat) a particularly dangerous and easy-to-miss memory leak, compared to a ThreadLocal used on a short-lived, one-off thread?
options: Pooled threads are reused across many requests and are never themselves garbage collected between requests, so a ThreadLocal value that isn't explicitly removed (e.g. in a finally block) stays reachable from that long-lived thread indefinitely, silently pinning objects from request N long after request N has completed
ThreadLocal values are always automatically cleared by the JVM at the end of every HTTP request, regardless of the server's threading model, so this scenario cannot actually occur
The leak only happens because ThreadLocal internally uses a static HashMap shared across all threads in the JVM
A ThreadLocal on a pooled thread is reclaimed immediately once the thread becomes idle, making this no more risky than a one-off thread
explanation: A one-off thread that finishes and terminates naturally takes its ThreadLocal values with it once the Thread object itself becomes unreachable, but a pooled thread is deliberately kept alive and reused for the next request -- since the live Thread is itself a GC Root, anything left in its ThreadLocal storage stays reachable across every subsequent request unless the code explicitly calls remove() (typically in a finally block), which is exactly why ThreadLocal cleanup is a recurring theme in production leak investigations.
